# value_bag - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/value-bag/

## Expand description

Structured values.

This crate contains the [ ValueBag](https://docs.rs/struct.ValueBag.html) type, a container for an anonymous structured value.

`ValueBag`s can be captured in various ways and then formatted, inspected, and serialized
without losing their original structure.The producer of a [ ValueBag](https://docs.rs/struct.ValueBag.html) may use a different strategy for capturing than the eventual
consumer. They don’t need to coordinate directly.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Error](https://docs.rs/struct.Error.html)
- An error encountered while working with structured data.
- [Owned](https://docs.rs/struct.OwnedValueBag.html)- Value - Bag
- A dynamic structured value.
- [Value](https://docs.rs/struct.ValueBag.html)- Bag
- A dynamic structured value.

# value-bag 1.12.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/value-bag/latest

`value-bag`

## What is a value bag?

A `ValueBag` is an anonymous structured value that supports casting, downcasting, formatting, and serializing. The producer of a `ValueBag` and its eventual consumer don't need to agree on a serialization contract. Any translation is handled internally by `ValueBag`.

Say we capture an `i32` using its `Display` implementation as a `ValueBag`:

```
let bag = capture_display;
```
That value can then be cast to a concrete integer type, like `u64`:

```
let num = bag.as_u64.unwrap;
assert_eq!;
```
It could also be serialized as a number using `serde`:

```
let num = to_value.unwrap;
assert!;
```
It works for more complex types too. Say we derive `sval::Value` on a type and capture it as a `ValueBag`:

```
let work = Work
let bag = capture_sval2;
```
We could still serialize that value using `serde` without losing structure:

```
let obj = to_value.unwrap;
assert!;
```
It could also be formatted using `Display`:

```
assert_eq!;
```
The tradeoff in all this is that `ValueBag` needs to depend on the serialization frameworks (`sval`, `serde`, and `std::fmt`) that it supports, instead of just providing an API of its own for others to plug into. Doing this lets `ValueBag` guarantee everything will always line up, and keep its own public API narrow.

## Getting started

Add the `value-bag` crate to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
version = "1.12.0"
```
You'll probably also want to add a feature for either `sval` (if you're in a no-std environment) or `serde` (if you need to integrate with other code that uses `serde`):

```
version = "1.12.0"
features =
```
```
version = "1.12.0"
features =
```
Then you're ready to capture anonymous values!

```
// Capture a value that implements `serde::Serialize`
let bag = capture_serde1;
// Print the contents of the value bag
println!;
```
## Cargo features

The `value-bag` crate is no-std by default, and offers the following Cargo features:

- `std`: Enable support for the standard library. This allows more types to be captured in a- `ValueBag`.
- `error`: Enable support for capturing- `std::error::Error`s. Implies- `std`.
- `sval`: Enable support for using the- `sval`- `ValueBag`s by implementing- `sval::value::Value`. Implies- `sval2`.- `sval2`: Enable support for the stable- `2.x.x`version of- `sval`.

- `serde`: Enable support for using the- `serde`- `ValueBag`s by implementing- `serde::Serialize`. Implies- `std`and- `serde1`.- `serde1`: Enable support for the stable- `1.x.x`version of- `serde`.

- `owned`: Add support for buffering- `ValueBag`s into an owned- `Send + Sync`variant.
- `seq`: Add support for working with sequences without needing to go through a full serialization framework.
- `test`: Add test helpers for inspecting the shape of the value inside a- `ValueBag`.

# wasm_bindgen - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/wasm-bindgen/^0.2/

## Expand description

Runtime support for the `wasm-bindgen` tool

This crate contains the runtime support necessary for `wasm-bindgen` the
attribute and tool. Crates pull in the `#[wasm_bindgen]` attribute through
this crate and this crate also provides JS bindings through the `JsValue`
interface.

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

[§](https://docs.rs#enable-interning)`enable-interning`

Enables the internal cache for [`wasm_bindgen::intern`].

This feature currently enables the `std` feature, meaning that it is not
compatible with `no_std` environments.

[§](https://docs.rs#std-default)`std` (default)

Enabling this feature will make the crate depend on the Rust standard library.

Disable this feature to use this crate in `no_std` environments.

[§](https://docs.rs#strict-macro)`strict-macro`

All warnings the `#[wasm_bindgen]` macro emits are turned into hard errors.
This mainly affects unused attribute options.

[§](https://docs.rs#deprecated-features)Deprecated features

[§](https://docs.rs#serde-serialize)`serde-serialize`

**Deprecated:** Use the [ serde-wasm-bindgen](https://docs.rs/serde-wasm-bindgen/latest/serde_wasm_bindgen/) crate instead.

Enables the `JsValue::from_serde` and `JsValue::into_serde` methods for
serializing and deserializing Rust types to and from JavaScript.

[§](https://docs.rs#spans)`spans`

**Deprecated:** This feature became a no-op in wasm-bindgen v0.2.20 (Sep 7, 2018).

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use crate::convert::`- [IntoJsGeneric](https://docs.rs/convert/trait.IntoJsGeneric.html);
- `pub use crate::convert::`- [JsGeneric](https://docs.rs/convert/trait.JsGeneric.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [closure](https://docs.rs/closure/index.html)
- Support for closures in `wasm-bindgen`
- [convert](https://docs.rs/convert/index.html)
- ⚠️ Unstable
- [prelude](https://docs.rs/prelude/index.html)
- A module which is typically glob imported.
- [sys](https://docs.rs/sys/index.html)
- JavaScript system types that are re-exported by `js-sys`.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [link_to](https://docs.rs/macro.link_to.html)
- This macro takes a JS module as input and returns a URL that can be used to access it at runtime.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Clamped](https://docs.rs/struct.Clamped.html)
- A wrapper type around slices and vectors for binding the `Uint8ClampedArray`array in JS.
- [JsError](https://docs.rs/struct.JsError.html)
- Convenience type for use on exported `fn() -> Result<T, JsError>`functions, where you wish to throw a JavaScript`Error`object.
- [JsStatic](https://docs.rs/struct.JsStatic.html)- Deprecated
- Wrapper type for imported statics.
- [JsThread](https://docs.rs/struct.JsThreadLocal.html)- Local
- Wrapper type for imported statics.
- [JsValue](https://docs.rs/struct.JsValue.html)
- Representation of an object owned by JS.
- [Parent](https://docs.rs/struct.Parent.html)
- Storage wrapper for the auto-injected `parent`field on a struct that declares`#[wasm_bindgen(extends = Parent)]`.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Erasable](https://docs.rs/trait.ErasableGeneric.html)- Generic
- Private marker trait for erasable generics - types with this trait have the same repr for all generic param values, and can therefore be transmuted on the singular Repr type representation on ABI boundaries.
- [JsCast](https://docs.rs/trait.JsCast.html)
- A trait for dynamic checked and unchecked casting between JS types.
- [Unwrap](https://docs.rs/trait.UnwrapThrowExt.html)- Throw - Ext
- An extension trait for `Option<T>`and`Result<T, E>`for unwrapping the`T`value, or throwing a JS error if it is not available.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [exports](https://docs.rs/fn.exports.html)
- Returns a handle to this Wasm instance’s `WebAssembly.Instance.prototype.exports`
- [externref_](https://docs.rs/fn.externref_heap_live_count.html)- heap_ - live_ - count
- Get the count of live `externref`s /`JsValue`s in`wasm-bindgen`’s heap.
- [function_](https://docs.rs/fn.function_table.html)- table
- Returns a handle to this Wasm instance’s `WebAssembly.Table`which is the indirect function table used by Rust
- [instance](https://docs.rs/fn.instance.html)
- Returns a handle to this Wasm instance’s `WebAssembly.Instance`. This is only available when the final Wasm app is built with`--target no-modules`,`--target web`,`--target deno`or`--target nodejs`. It is unavailable for`--target bundler`.
- [intern](https://docs.rs/fn.intern.html)
- Interns Rust strings so that it’s much faster to send them to JS.
- [memory](https://docs.rs/fn.memory.html)
- Returns a handle to this Wasm instance’s `WebAssembly.Memory`
- [module](https://docs.rs/fn.module.html)
- Returns a handle to this Wasm instance’s `WebAssembly.Module`. This is only available when the final Wasm app is built with`--target no-modules`,`--target web`,`--target deno`or`--target nodejs`. It is unavailable for`--target bundler`.
- [throw_](https://docs.rs/fn.throw_str.html)- str
- Throws a JS exception.
- [throw_](https://docs.rs/fn.throw_val.html)- val
- Rethrow a JS exception
- [unintern](https://docs.rs/fn.unintern.html)
- Removes a Rust string from the intern cache.

# About Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/about

Docs.rs is an
            [open source](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs)
            documentation host for crates of the
            [Rust Programming Language](https://www.rust-lang.org/).
            All libraries published to [crates.io](https://crates.io)
            are documented. If you just published a crate, your crate is likely
            still in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

            The source code of Docs.rs is available on
            [GitHub](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs). If
            you ever encounter an issue, don't hesitate to report it! (And
            thanks in advance!)

Currently running Docs.rs version is: **0.0.0 (964c90a45859fd8f9076e3cbe58470a5a4f4d4f7 2026-07-01 )**

Summaries of the documentation build processes [are available at /releases/](https://docs.rs/releases).

            JavaScript in support of documentation is allowed but not guaranteed to work on docs.rs. What that
            means: If you write documentation that inlines some JavaScript (like
            [KaTeX](https://katex.org/)), that's allowed, and
            will probably work today but may break in the future.

However, it's not allowed to put JavaScript or other content in docs published on docs.rs for the purpose of tracking visitors. For instance, adding Google Analytics scripts, tracking pixels, or site verification for services like Google Search Console. Crates that do this will have the relevant versions removed and may be blocked from docs.rs.

            Docs.rs is run and maintained by the [Docs.rs team](https://www.rust-lang.org/governance/teams/dev-tools#team-docs-rs).
            You can find us in #t-docs-rs on [Zulip](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/stream/356853-t-docs-rs).

# Builds

Source: https://docs.rs/about/builds

Docs.rs automatically builds documentation for crates released on [crates.io](https://crates.io/).
                It may take a while to build your crate, depending on how many crates are in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

                All crates are built in a sandbox using the nightly release of the Rust compiler.
                The current version in use is `rustc 1.98.0-nightly (4c9d2bfe4 2026-07-01)`.

                The README displayed on docs.rs follows Cargo’s `package.readme` rules.
                If `readme` is not set, docs.rs will look for `README.md`, `README.txt`, or `README` in the crate root.
                Set `readme = "path/to/file"` to use a custom file, `readme = true` to use `README.md`, or `readme = false` to disable the README.

                To recognize Docs.rs from your Rust code, you can test for the `docsrs` cfg, e.g.:

```
```
                To recognize Docs.rs from `build.rs` files, you can test for the environment variable `DOCS_RS`, e.g.:

`if var.is_ok `
              All targets other than `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` are cross-compiled. For implementation reasons, this is unlikely to change for the foreseeable future.

                You can configure how your crate is built by adding [package metadata](https://docs.rs/metadata) to your `Cargo.toml`, e.g.:

```
[]
 = ["--cfg", "my_cfg"]
```
`#[cfg(my_cfg)]` (not to be confused with `#[cfg(doc)]`) can be used for conditional compilation.
                This approach is also useful for setting
                When you start using docs.rs metadata or `#[cfg(docsrs)]` in your code, you might run into issues
                where your code builds fine locally but fails on docs.rs.
                To avoid this, you can add [ cargo docs-rs](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-docs-rs) to
                your test-suite.
                While it doesn't perfectly replicate our build environment, it can catch many common issues.

                The Docs.rs [README](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/blob/master/README.md#build-subcommand) describes how to build
                unpublished crate documentation locally using the same build environment as the Docs.rs build agent.

                Missing dependencies are a common reason for failed builds.
                Docs.rs dependencies are managed through
                [crates-build-env](https://github.com/rust-lang/crates-build-env).
                See [Forge](https://forge.rust-lang.org/docs-rs/add-dependencies.html) for how to add a dependency.

                Most of the sandbox is a read-only file system, including the source directory of your crate and its dependencies.
                If your `build.rs` generates files that are relevant for documentation, consider writing to the
                [cargo output directory](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/environment-variables.html#environment-variables-cargo-sets-for-crates),
                passed in the environment variable `OUT_DIR`.

All the builds are executed inside a sandbox with limited resources. The current limits are:

| Available RAM | 6.44 GB |
| Maximum rustdoc execution time | 15m |
| Maximum size of a build log | 102.4 kB |
| Network access | blocked |
| Maximum number of build targets | 10 |

                If your build fails because it hit one of these limits, please
                [open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose)
                to get them increased for your crate.
                Since our build agent has finite resources, we have to consider each case individually. However, there are a few general policies:

If your crate fails to build for a reason not listed here, you can rebuild it from [crates.io](https://crates.io) website as you can see below:

Or you can [file an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues) if you think it's a **docs.rs** issue.

# Metadata

Source: https://docs.rs/about/metadata

You can customize docs.rs builds by defining `[package.metadata.docs.rs]`
		table in your crates' `Cargo.toml`.

The available configuration flags you can customize are:

```
[]
 = "test"
[]
# Features to pass to Cargo (default: [])
 = ["feature1", "feature2"]
# Whether to pass `--all-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Whether to pass `--no-default-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Target to test build on, used as the default landing page (default: "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu")
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
 = "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu"
# Targets to build (default: see below)
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
#
# Default targets:
# - x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - aarch64-apple-darwin
# - x86_64-pc-windows-msvc
# - aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - i686-pc-windows-msvc
#
# Set this to `[]` to only build the default target.
#
# If `default-target` is unset, the first element of `targets` is treated as the default target.
# Otherwise, these `targets` are built in addition to the default target.
# If both `default-target` and `targets` are unset,
#   all tier-one targets will be built and `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` will be used as the default target.
 = ["aarch64-apple-darwin", "x86_64-pc-windows-msvc"]
# If you want to instead add another target without overwriting the default ones:
 = ["i686-apple-darwin"]
# Additional `RUSTFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustc-arg"]
# Additional `RUSTDOCFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustdoc-arg"]
# List of command line arguments for `cargo`.
#
# These cannot be a subcommand, they may only be options.
 = ["-Z", "build-std"]
```

# Shorthand URLs

Source: https://docs.rs/about/redirections

Docs.rs uses semver to parse URLs. You can use this feature to access
            crates' documentation easily. Example of URL redirections for
            `clap` crate:

| URL | Redirects to documentation of |
|---|---|
| [docs.rs/clap](https://docs.rs/clap) | Latest version of clap |
| [docs.rs/clap::Command](https://docs.rs/clap::Command) | Latest version of clap, and search for "Command" within the crate |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2) | 2.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2.9](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2.9) | 2.9.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/2.9.3](https://docs.rs/clap/2.9.3) | 2.9.3 version (you don't need `=`unlike semver) |
| [docs.rs/clap/*](https://docs.rs/clap/*) | Latest version of this page (if it still exists). "latest" or "newest" work as well as `*`. |

# Download

Source: https://docs.rs/about/download

docs.rs stores the `rustdoc` output in a ZIP file.

                These archives can be used as a base for further processing of
                the documentation for offline readers like Dash or Zeal.
                **They are not directly usable for offline documentation.**

The download is possible for specific or semantic versions:

But also viaTo unpack the ZIP file you need any zip utility that supports PKZIP version 4.6 and BZIP2 & Deflate compression.

The archives will contain all the documentation HTML files for all targets and CSS/JS assets that are specific to the build. The default target will be found at the root, and other targets each in its own subfolder.

                Docs.rs is running rustdoc with `--static-root-path "/-/rustdoc.static/"`,
                which leads to all references to static assets breaking if they are not
                available under that path. Older builds used `--static-root-path "/"`, which
                means you will have to handle both.

                Since we're also adding `--emit=invocation-specific` to our build
                the archives will *not* contain any static assets that are specific to the
                toolchain. For now these will have to be downloaded file-by-file directly
                from docs.rs.

---

# Rustdoc JSON

Source: https://docs.rs/about/rustdoc-json

docs.rs builds & hosts the [ rustdoc JSON](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustdoc/unstable-features.html#json-output) output.

This structured version of the documentation can be used for inspecting the docs and types of the crate in a programmatic way.

                The JSON file you're downloading might have been built with an older version of `rustdoc`
                so you might have to check the `format_version` attribute to determine how to parse the structure.
                The [ rustdoc-types](https://docs.rs/rustdoc-types/) crate helps with this.

**
                We started building rustdoc JSON on 2025-05-23. So any release before that won't have a download
                available until our rebuilds reached that release.
            **

                The download URLs can be generic or specific, depending on what you need. In case of rebuilds we
                also keep old format versions around. **Until we rebuilt all releases, we might return
                a `404 NOT FOUND` for some.**

By default we use `zstd` compression, which is more space efficient and faster to decompress. For more limited environments we also started supporting `gzip` compression. You can receive gzip by adding `.gz` to the given URL.

Here some URL examples you can use.

| URL | Redirects to JSON download of |
|---|---|
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json) | latest version, default target, latest format-version |

# hanzo_ml - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/hanzo-ml/0.11.41/hanzo_ml/

## Expand description

ML framework for Rust

```
use hanzo_ml::{Tensor, DType, Device};
let a = Tensor::arange(0f32, 6f32, &Device::Cpu)?.reshape((2, 3))?;
let b = Tensor::arange(0f32, 12f32, &Device::Cpu)?.reshape((3, 4))?;
let c = a.matmul(&b)?;
```
[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

- Simple syntax (looks and feels like PyTorch)
- CPU and Cuda backends (and M1 support)
- Enable serverless (CPU) small and fast deployments
- Model training
- Distributed computing (NCCL).
- Models out of the box (Llama, Whisper, Falcon, …)

[§](https://docs.rs#faq)FAQ

- Why Hanzo?

Hanzo stems from the need to reduce binary size in order to *enable serverless*
possible by making the whole engine smaller than PyTorch very large library volume

And simply *removing Python* from production workloads.
Python can really add overhead in more complex workflows and the [GIL](https://www.backblaze.com/blog/the-python-gil-past-present-and-future/) is a notorious source of headaches.

Rust is cool, and a lot of the HF ecosystem already has Rust crates [safetensors](https://github.com/huggingface/safetensors) and [tokenizers](https://github.com/huggingface/tokenizers)

[§](https://docs.rs#other-crates)Other Crates

Hanzo consists of a number of crates. This crate holds core the common data structures but you may wish to look at the docs for the other crates which can be found here:

- [hanzo-ml](https://docs.rs/hanzo-ml/). Core Datastructures and DataTypes.
- [hanzo-nn](https://docs.rs/hanzo-nn/). Building blocks for Neural Nets.
- [hanzo-datasets](https://docs.rs/hanzo-datasets/). Rust access to commonly used Datasets like MNIST.
- [hanzo-ml-examples](https://docs.rs/hanzo-ml-examples/). Examples of Hanzo in Use.
- [hanzo-onnx](https://docs.rs/hanzo-onnx/). Loading and using ONNX models.
- [hanzo-ml-pyo3](https://docs.rs/hanzo-ml-pyo3/). Access to Hanzo from Python.
- [hanzo-transformers](https://docs.rs/hanzo-transformers/). Hanzo implementation of many published transformer models.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [backend](https://docs.rs/backend/index.html)
- Traits to Define Backend Behavior
- [backprop](https://docs.rs/backprop/index.html)
- Methods for backpropagation of gradients.
- [compute](https://docs.rs/compute/index.html)
- Compute policy — the one place a model decides how its activations flow.
- [conv](https://docs.rs/conv/index.html)
- 1D and 2D Convolutions
- [cpu](https://docs.rs/cpu/index.html)
- Traits and methods for CPU-backed Tensors
- [cpu_](https://docs.rs/cpu_backend/index.html)- backend
- Implementation of Backend Fns for CPU
- [display](https://docs.rs/display/index.html)
- Pretty printing of tensors
- [dummy_](https://docs.rs/dummy_cuda_backend/index.html)- cuda_ - backend
- Implementation of the Cuda backend when Cuda support has not been compiled in.
- [dummy_](https://docs.rs/dummy_dtype/index.html)- dtype
- Dummy data types for experimental/future float formats
- [dummy_](https://docs.rs/dummy_vulkan_backend/index.html)- vulkan_ - backend
- [dummy_](https://docs.rs/dummy_wgpu_backend/index.html)- wgpu_ - backend
- [error](https://docs.rs/error/index.html)
- Hanzo-specific Error and Result
- [fattn_](https://docs.rs/fattn_decode/index.html)- decode
- Fused F32 head_dim-512 online-softmax flash-decode attention.
- [layout](https://docs.rs/layout/index.html)
- Tensor Layouts including contiguous or sparse strides
- [model_](https://docs.rs/model_delta/index.html)- delta
- Model merging and delta-compression utilities, implemented natively on top of
the `hanzo-ml`tensor + safetensors APIs (no Python, no external tooling).
- [npy](https://docs.rs/npy/index.html)
- Numpy support for tensors.
- [op](https://docs.rs/op/index.html)
- Tensor Operation Enums and Traits
- [pickle](https://docs.rs/pickle/index.html)
- Just enough pickle support to be able to read PyTorch checkpoints.
- [quantized](https://docs.rs/quantized/index.html)
- [safetensors](https://docs.rs/safetensors/index.html)
- Module to load `safetensor`files into CPU/GPU memory.
- [scalar](https://docs.rs/scalar/index.html)
- TensorScalar Enum and Trait
- [shape](https://docs.rs/shape/index.html)
- The shape of a tensor is a tuple with the size of each of its dimensions.
- [streaming](https://docs.rs/streaming/index.html)
- StreamTensror useful for streaming ops.
- [test_](https://docs.rs/test_utils/index.html)- utils
- [utils](https://docs.rs/utils/index.html)
- Useful functions for checking features.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [bail](https://docs.rs/macro.bail.html)
- [for_](https://docs.rs/macro.for_each_quant.html)- each_ - quant
- A single declarative table of every quant type, driving the `mod.rs`wiring so that`from_u32`/`to_u32`/`cpu_zeros`/`from_data`/`type_size`/`block_size`are generated from ONE list instead of six hand-maintained`match`blocks.
- [map_](https://docs.rs/macro.map_dtype.html)- dtype

- [DType](https://docs.rs/struct.DTypeParseError.html)- Parse - Error

# sortcrab - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sortcrab/0.1.3/sortcrab/

## Expand description

sortcrab — file organization library.

sortcrab scans a source directory, classifies each file by its extension,
computes an academic semester from the file’s modification time, and moves
it into a structured destination tree:
`{target}/{category}/{subcategory}/{semester}/{filename}`.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use sortcrab::core::sort_files;
use sortcrab::config::rules::RulesConfig;
use sortcrab::config::SemesterConfig;
use std::path::Path;
let rules = RulesConfig::default();
let semester = SemesterConfig::default();
let report = sort_files(
    Path::new("/path/to/source"),
    Path::new("/path/to/target"),
    &rules,
    false,
    &semester,
)?;
println!("Moved {} files", report.moved);
```
## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [cli](https://docs.rs/cli/index.html)
- CLI argument parsing and command dispatch.
- [config](https://docs.rs/config/index.html)
- Configuration loading, saving, and path resolution.
- [core](https://docs.rs/core/index.html)
- Core domain logic: classification, file moving, semester computation, and orchestration.
- [error](https://docs.rs/error/index.html)
- Error types for sortcrab operations.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [init_](https://docs.rs/fn.init_logging.html)- logging
- Initialize logging based on verbosity level.
- [run](https://docs.rs/fn.run.html)
- Run the sortcrab CLI.

# winit - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/fission-winit/0.30.13-fission.1/winit/

## Expand description

Winit is a cross-platform window creation and event loop management library.

[§](https://docs.rs#building-windows)Building windows

Before you can create a [ Window](https://docs.rs/window/struct.Window.html), you first need to build an

[. This is done with the](https://docs.rs/event_loop/struct.EventLoop.html)

`EventLoop`[function.](https://docs.rs/event_loop/struct.EventLoop.html#method.new)

`EventLoop::new()````
use winit::event_loop::EventLoop;
fn main() {
    let event_loop = EventLoop::new().unwrap();
    // ...
}
```
Then you create a [ Window](https://docs.rs/window/struct.Window.html) with

[.](https://docs.rs/event_loop/struct.ActiveEventLoop.html#method.create_window)

`create_window`[§](https://docs.rs#event-handling)Event handling

Once a [ Window](https://docs.rs/window/struct.Window.html) has been created, it will generate different

*events*. A

[object can generate](https://docs.rs/window/struct.Window.html)

`Window`[s when certain input events occur, such as a cursor moving over the window or a key getting pressed while the window is focused. Devices can generate](https://docs.rs/event/enum.WindowEvent.html)

`WindowEvent`[s, which contain unfiltered event data that isn’t specific to a certain window. Some user activity, like mouse movement, can generate both a](https://docs.rs/event/enum.DeviceEvent.html)

`DeviceEvent`

`WindowEvent`*and*a

[. You can also create and handle your own custom](https://docs.rs/event/enum.DeviceEvent.html)

`DeviceEvent`[s, if desired.](https://docs.rs/event/enum.Event.html#variant.UserEvent)

`Event::UserEvent`You can retrieve events by calling [ EventLoop::run_app()](https://docs.rs/event_loop/struct.EventLoop.html#method.run_app). This function will
dispatch events for every

[that was created with that particular](https://docs.rs/window/struct.Window.html)

`Window`[, and will run until](https://docs.rs/event_loop/struct.EventLoop.html)

`EventLoop`[is used, at which point](https://docs.rs/event_loop/struct.ActiveEventLoop.html#method.exit)

`exit()`[.](https://docs.rs/event/enum.Event.html#variant.LoopExiting)

`Event::LoopExiting`Winit no longer uses a `EventLoop::poll_events() -> impl Iterator<Event>`-based event loop
model, since that can’t be implemented properly on some platforms (e.g web, iOS) and works
poorly on most other platforms. However, this model can be re-implemented to an extent with
`EventLoopExtPumpEvents::pump_app_events()` 1. See that method’s documentation for more reasons about why
it’s discouraged beyond compatibility reasons.

```
use winit::application::ApplicationHandler;
use winit::event::WindowEvent;
use winit::event_loop::{ActiveEventLoop, ControlFlow, EventLoop};
use winit::window::{Window, WindowId};
#[derive(Default)]
struct App {
    window: Option<Window>,
}
impl ApplicationHandler for App {
    fn resumed(&mut self, event_loop: &ActiveEventLoop) {
        self.window = Some(event_loop.create_window(Window::default_attributes()).unwrap());
    }
    fn window_event(&mut self, event_loop: &ActiveEventLoop, id: WindowId, event: WindowEvent) {
        match event {
            WindowEvent::CloseRequested => {
                println!("The close button was pressed; stopping");
                event_loop.exit();
            },
            WindowEvent::RedrawRequested => {
                // Redraw the application.
                //
                // It's preferable for applications that do not render continuously to render in
                // this event rather than in AboutToWait, since rendering in here allows
                // the program to gracefully handle redraws requested by the OS.
                // Draw.
                // Queue a RedrawRequested event.
                //
                // You only need to call this if you've determined that you need to redraw in
                // applications which do not always need to. Applications that redraw continuously
                // can render here instead.
                self.window.as_ref().unwrap().request_redraw();
            }
            _ => (),
        }
    }
}
fn main() {
    let event_loop = EventLoop::new().unwrap();
    // ControlFlow::Poll continuously runs the event loop, even if the OS hasn't
    // dispatched any events. This is ideal for games and similar applications.
    event_loop.set_control_flow(ControlFlow::Poll);
    // ControlFlow::Wait pauses the event loop if no events are available to process.
    // This is ideal for non-game applications that only update in response to user
    // input, and uses significantly less power/CPU time than ControlFlow::Poll.
    event_loop.set_control_flow(ControlFlow::Wait);
    let mut app = App::default();
    event_loop.run_app(&mut app);
}
```
[ WindowEvent](https://docs.rs/event/enum.WindowEvent.html) has a

[member. In multi-window environments, it should be compared to the value returned by](https://docs.rs/window/struct.WindowId.html)

`WindowId`[to determine which](https://docs.rs/window/struct.Window.html#method.id)

`Window::id()`[dispatched the event.](https://docs.rs/window/struct.Window.html)

`Window`[§](https://docs.rs#drawing-on-the-window)Drawing on the window

Winit doesn’t directly provide any methods for drawing on a [ Window](https://docs.rs/window/struct.Window.html). However, it allows you
to retrieve the raw handle of the window and display (see the

[module and/or the](https://docs.rs/platform/index.html)

`platform`[and](https://docs.rs/window/struct.Window.html#method.raw_window_handle)

`raw_window_handle`[methods), which in turn allows you to create an OpenGL/Vulkan/DirectX/Metal/etc. context that can be used to render graphics.](https://docs.rs/window/struct.Window.html#method.raw_display_handle)

`raw_display_handle`Note that many platforms will display garbage data in the window’s client area if the
application doesn’t render anything to the window by the time the desktop compositor is ready to
display the window to the user. If you notice this happening, you should create the window with
[ visible set to false](https://docs.rs/window/struct.WindowAttributes.html#method.with_visible) and explicitly make
the window visible only once you’re ready to render into it.

[§](https://docs.rs#ui-scaling)UI scaling

UI scaling is important, go read the docs for the [ dpi](https://docs.rs/dpi/index.html) crate for an
introduction.

All of Winit’s functions return physical types, but can take either logical or physical coordinates as input, allowing you to use the most convenient coordinate system for your particular application.

Winit will dispatch a [ ScaleFactorChanged](https://docs.rs/event/enum.WindowEvent.html#variant.ScaleFactorChanged) event whenever a window’s scale factor has changed.
This can happen if the user drags their window from a standard-resolution monitor to a high-DPI
monitor or if the user changes their DPI settings. This allows you to rescale your application’s
UI elements and adjust how the platform changes the window’s size to reflect the new scale
factor. If a window hasn’t received a

[event, its scale factor can be found by calling](https://docs.rs/event/enum.WindowEvent.html#variant.ScaleFactorChanged)

`ScaleFactorChanged`[.](https://docs.rs/window/struct.Window.html#method.scale_factor)

`window.scale_factor()`[§](https://docs.rs#cargo-features)Cargo Features

Winit provides the following Cargo features:

- `x11`(enabled by default): On Unix platforms, enables the X11 backend.
- `wayland`(enabled by default): On Unix platforms, enables the Wayland backend.
- `rwh_04`: Implement- `raw-window-handle v0.4`traits.
- `rwh_05`: Implement- `raw-window-handle v0.5`traits.
- `rwh_06`: Implement- `raw-window-handle v0.6`traits.
- `serde`: Enables serialization/deserialization of certain types with- [Serde](https://crates.io/crates/serde).
- `mint`: Enables mint (math interoperability standard types) conversions.

See the [ platform](https://docs.rs/platform/index.html) module for documentation on platform-specific cargo
features.

# hanzo-kernel 0.2.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/hanzo-kernel/0.2.0

Please check the

[build logs](https://docs.rs/crate/hanzo-kernel/0.2.0/builds)for more information.

See

[Builds](https://docs.rs/about/builds)for ideas on how to fix a failed build, or

[Metadata](https://docs.rs/about/metadata)for how to configure docs.rs builds.

If you believe this is docs.rs' fault,

[open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose).

hanzo-kernel: Hanzo's first-party GPU kernel DSL.

Write a kernel ONCE in Rust; it lowers to CUDA / ROCm / Vulkan / Metal. This crate is the
first-party facade over the CubeCL lowering engine: kernel source names only `hanzo_kernel::*`,
never `cubecl`. "Values, not places" -- CubeCL is the implementation value; `hanzo_kernel` is the
stable namespace we build against, so the engine can be upgraded (or forked) without touching a
single kernel.

The perf primitives our hand-tuned kernels rely on are all here and lower to the native instruction on each backend:

- `dot`on a vectorized- `Line<i8>`-> dp4a / OpSDotAccSat (int8 4-way dot)
- `cmma`-> tensor cores (WMMA / cooperative-matrix / simdgroup)
- `SharedMemory`,- `plane_*`(subgroup reduce/shuffle),- `Atomic`, barriers

MIGRATION POLICY (perf-gated, never a downgrade): the DSL provides COVERAGE -- every quant type on every backend, from one source, killing the "same op, N impls, N numeric behaviors" bug class. A hand-tuned kernel is replaced by its DSL twin ONLY when the DSL version is bit-exact AND within perf noise (bench-gated). Where a hand-tuned kernel still wins, it stays as the specialized peak path and the DSL is the portable fallback for the backends that lack a tuned version.

---

# value-bag 1.12.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/value-bag/1.12.0

`value-bag`

## What is a value bag?

A `ValueBag` is an anonymous structured value that supports casting, downcasting, formatting, and serializing. The producer of a `ValueBag` and its eventual consumer don't need to agree on a serialization contract. Any translation is handled internally by `ValueBag`.

Say we capture an `i32` using its `Display` implementation as a `ValueBag`:

```
let bag = capture_display;
```
That value can then be cast to a concrete integer type, like `u64`:

```
let num = bag.as_u64.unwrap;
assert_eq!;
```
It could also be serialized as a number using `serde`:

```
let num = to_value.unwrap;
assert!;
```
It works for more complex types too. Say we derive `sval::Value` on a type and capture it as a `ValueBag`:

```
let work = Work
let bag = capture_sval2;
```
We could still serialize that value using `serde` without losing structure:

```
let obj = to_value.unwrap;
assert!;
```
It could also be formatted using `Display`:

```
assert_eq!;
```
The tradeoff in all this is that `ValueBag` needs to depend on the serialization frameworks (`sval`, `serde`, and `std::fmt`) that it supports, instead of just providing an API of its own for others to plug into. Doing this lets `ValueBag` guarantee everything will always line up, and keep its own public API narrow.

## Getting started

Add the `value-bag` crate to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
version = "1.12.0"
```
You'll probably also want to add a feature for either `sval` (if you're in a no-std environment) or `serde` (if you need to integrate with other code that uses `serde`):

```
version = "1.12.0"
features =
```
```
version = "1.12.0"
features =
```
Then you're ready to capture anonymous values!

```
// Capture a value that implements `serde::Serialize`
let bag = capture_serde1;
// Print the contents of the value bag
println!;
```
## Cargo features

The `value-bag` crate is no-std by default, and offers the following Cargo features:

- `std`: Enable support for the standard library. This allows more types to be captured in a- `ValueBag`.
- `error`: Enable support for capturing- `std::error::Error`s. Implies- `std`.
- `sval`: Enable support for using the- `sval`- `ValueBag`s by implementing- `sval::value::Value`. Implies- `sval2`.- `sval2`: Enable support for the stable- `2.x.x`version of- `sval`.

- `serde`: Enable support for using the- `serde`- `ValueBag`s by implementing- `serde::Serialize`. Implies- `std`and- `serde1`.- `serde1`: Enable support for the stable- `1.x.x`version of- `serde`.

- `owned`: Add support for buffering- `ValueBag`s into an owned- `Send + Sync`variant.
- `seq`: Add support for working with sequences without needing to go through a full serialization framework.
- `test`: Add test helpers for inspecting the shape of the value inside a- `ValueBag`.

---

# value_bag - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/value-bag/1.12.0/target-redirect/value_bag/

## Expand description

Structured values.

This crate contains the [ ValueBag](https://docs.rs/struct.ValueBag.html) type, a container for an anonymous structured value.

`ValueBag`s can be captured in various ways and then formatted, inspected, and serialized
without losing their original structure.The producer of a [ ValueBag](https://docs.rs/struct.ValueBag.html) may use a different strategy for capturing than the eventual
consumer. They don’t need to coordinate directly.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Error](https://docs.rs/struct.Error.html)
- An error encountered while working with structured data.
- [Owned](https://docs.rs/struct.OwnedValueBag.html)- Value - Bag
- A dynamic structured value.
- [Value](https://docs.rs/struct.ValueBag.html)- Bag
- A dynamic structured value.

# value_bag/lib.rs

[1](https://docs.rs#1)//! Structured values.
[2](https://docs.rs#2)//!
[3](https://docs.rs#3)//! This crate contains the [`ValueBag`] type, a container for an anonymous structured value.
[4](https://docs.rs#4)//! `ValueBag`s can be captured in various ways and then formatted, inspected, and serialized
[5](https://docs.rs#5)//! without losing their original structure.
[6](https://docs.rs#6)//!
[7](https://docs.rs#7)//! The producer of a [`ValueBag`] may use a different strategy for capturing than the eventual
[8](https://docs.rs#8)//! consumer. They don't need to coordinate directly.
[9](https://docs.rs#9)
[10](https://docs.rs#10)#![doc(html_root_url = "https://docs.rs/value-bag/1.12.0")]
[11](https://docs.rs#11)#![no_std]
[12](https://docs.rs#12)#![allow(
[13](https://docs.rs#13)    clippy::unnecessary_fallible_conversions,

[16](https://docs.rs#16))]
[17](https://docs.rs#17)
[18](https://docs.rs#18)/*
[19](https://docs.rs#19)# Crate design
[20](https://docs.rs#20)
[21](https://docs.rs#21)This library internally ties several frameworks together. The details of how
[22](https://docs.rs#22)this is done are hidden from end-users. It looks roughly like this:
[23](https://docs.rs#23)
[24](https://docs.rs#24)            ┌─────┐     ┌──────┐
[25](https://docs.rs#25)            │sval2│     │serde1│  1. libs on crates.io
[26](https://docs.rs#26)            └──┬──┘     └─┬─┬──┘
[27](https://docs.rs#27)               ├──────────┘ │
[28](https://docs.rs#28)       ┌───────▼──┐     ┌───▼───────┐
[29](https://docs.rs#29)       │meta/sval2│     │meta/serde1│  2. meta crates with features
[30](https://docs.rs#30)       └───────┬──┘     └───┬───────┘
[31](https://docs.rs#31)               │            │
[32](https://docs.rs#32) ┌─────────────▼──┐     ┌───▼─────────────┐
[33](https://docs.rs#33) │internal/sval/v2◄─────┤internal/serde/v1│  3. internal modules with `InternalVisitor`
[34](https://docs.rs#34) └─────────────┬──┘     └───┬─────────────┘
[35](https://docs.rs#35)               │            │
[36](https://docs.rs#36)        ┌──────▼────────┬───▼────────────┐
[37](https://docs.rs#37)        │Internal::Sval2│Internal::Serde1│  4. variants in `Internal` enum
[38](https://docs.rs#38)        └───────────────┼────────────────┘
[39](https://docs.rs#39)                        │
[40](https://docs.rs#40)┌───────────────────────▼────────────────────────┐
[41](https://docs.rs#41)│ValueBag::capture_sval2│ValueBag::capture_serde1│  5. ctors on `ValueBag`
[42](https://docs.rs#42)└───────────────────────┼────────────────────────┘
[43](https://docs.rs#43)                        │
[44](https://docs.rs#44)┌───────────────────────▼───────────────────────────┐
[45](https://docs.rs#45)│impl Value for ValueBag│impl Serialize for ValueBag│  6. trait impls on `ValueBag`
[46](https://docs.rs#46)└───────────────────────┴───────────────────────────┘
[47](https://docs.rs#47)
[48](https://docs.rs#48)## 1. libs on crates.io
[49](https://docs.rs#49)
[50](https://docs.rs#50)These are the frameworks like `serde` or `sval`.
[51](https://docs.rs#51)
[52](https://docs.rs#52)## 2. meta crates with features
[53](https://docs.rs#53)
[54](https://docs.rs#54)These are crates that are internal to `value-bag`. They depend on the public
[55](https://docs.rs#55)framework and any utility crates that come along with it. They also expose
[56](https://docs.rs#56)features for any other framework. This is done this way so `value-bag` can use
[57](https://docs.rs#57)Cargo's `crate?/feature` syntax to conditionally add framework support.
[58](https://docs.rs#58)
[59](https://docs.rs#59)## 3. internal modules with `InternalVisitor`
[60](https://docs.rs#60)
[61](https://docs.rs#61)These are modules in `value-bag` that integrate the framework using the
[62](https://docs.rs#62)`InternalVisitor` trait. This makes it possible for that framework to cast
[63](https://docs.rs#63)primitive values and pass-through any other framework.
[64](https://docs.rs#64)
[65](https://docs.rs#65)## 4. variants in `Internal` enum
[66](https://docs.rs#66)
[67](https://docs.rs#67)These are individual variants on the `Internal` enum that the `ValueBag`
[68](https://docs.rs#68)type wraps. Each framework has one or more variants in this enum.
[69](https://docs.rs#69)
[70](https://docs.rs#70)## 5. ctors on `ValueBag`
[71](https://docs.rs#71)
[72](https://docs.rs#72)These are constructors for producers of `ValueBag`s that accept a value
[73](https://docs.rs#73)implementing a serialization trait from a specific framework, like
[74](https://docs.rs#74)`serde::Serialize` or `sval::Value`.
[75](https://docs.rs#75)
[76](https://docs.rs#76)## 7. trait impls on `ValueBag`
[77](https://docs.rs#77)
[78](https://docs.rs#78)These are trait impls for consumers of `ValueBag`s that serialize the
[79](https://docs.rs#79)underlying value, bridging it if it was produced for a different framework.
[80](https://docs.rs#80)*/
[81](https://docs.rs#81)

[129](https://docs.rs#129)
[130](https://docs.rs#130)/// A dynamic structured value.
[131](https://docs.rs#131)///
[132](https://docs.rs#132)/// # Capturing values
[133](https://docs.rs#133)///
[134](https://docs.rs#134)/// There are a few ways to capture a value:
[135](https://docs.rs#135)///
[136](https://docs.rs#136)/// - Using the `ValueBag::capture_*` and `ValueBag::from_*` methods.
[137](https://docs.rs#137)/// - Using the standard `From` trait.
[138](https://docs.rs#138)/// - Using the `Fill` API.
[139](https://docs.rs#139)///
[140](https://docs.rs#140)/// ## Using the `ValueBag::capture_*` methods
[141](https://docs.rs#141)///
[142](https://docs.rs#142)/// `ValueBag` offers a few constructor methods that capture values of different kinds.
[143](https://docs.rs#143)/// These methods require a `T: 'static` to support downcasting.
[144](https://docs.rs#144)///
[145](https://docs.rs#145)/// ```
[146](https://docs.rs#146)/// use value_bag::ValueBag;
[147](https://docs.rs#147)///
[148](https://docs.rs#148)/// let value = ValueBag::capture_debug(&42i32);
[149](https://docs.rs#149)///
[150](https://docs.rs#150)/// assert_eq!(Some(42), value.to_i64());
[151](https://docs.rs#151)/// ```
[152](https://docs.rs#152)///
[153](https://docs.rs#153)/// Capturing a value using these methods will retain type information so that
[154](https://docs.rs#154)/// the contents of the bag can be serialized using an appropriate type.
[155](https://docs.rs#155)///
[156](https://docs.rs#156)/// For cases where the `'static` bound can't be satisfied, there's also a few
[157](https://docs.rs#157)/// constructors that exclude it.
[158](https://docs.rs#158)///
[159](https://docs.rs#159)/// ```
[160](https://docs.rs#160)/// # use std::fmt::Debug;
[161](https://docs.rs#161)/// use value_bag::ValueBag;
[162](https://docs.rs#162)///
[163](https://docs.rs#163)/// let value = ValueBag::from_debug(&42i32);
[164](https://docs.rs#164)///
[165](https://docs.rs#165)/// assert_eq!(None, value.to_i64());
[166](https://docs.rs#166)/// ```
[167](https://docs.rs#167)///
[168](https://docs.rs#168)/// These `ValueBag::from_*` methods are lossy though and `ValueBag::capture_*` should be preferred.
[169](https://docs.rs#169)///
[170](https://docs.rs#170)/// ## Using the standard `From` trait
[171](https://docs.rs#171)///
[172](https://docs.rs#172)/// Primitive types can be converted into a `ValueBag` using the standard `From` trait.
[173](https://docs.rs#173)///
[174](https://docs.rs#174)/// ```
[175](https://docs.rs#175)/// use value_bag::ValueBag;
[176](https://docs.rs#176)///
[177](https://docs.rs#177)/// let value = ValueBag::from(42i32);
[178](https://docs.rs#178)///
[179](https://docs.rs#179)/// assert_eq!(Some(42), value.to_i64());
[180](https://docs.rs#180)/// ```
[181](https://docs.rs#181)///
[182](https://docs.rs#182)/// ## Using the `Fill` API
[183](https://docs.rs#183)///
[184](https://docs.rs#184)/// The [`fill`] module provides a way to bridge APIs that may not be directly
[185](https://docs.rs#185)/// compatible with other constructor methods.
[186](https://docs.rs#186)///
[187](https://docs.rs#187)/// The `Fill` trait is automatically implemented for closures, so can usually
[188](https://docs.rs#188)/// be used in libraries that can't implement the trait themselves.
[189](https://docs.rs#189)///
[190](https://docs.rs#190)/// ```
[191](https://docs.rs#191)/// use value_bag::{ValueBag, fill::Slot};
[192](https://docs.rs#192)///
[193](https://docs.rs#193)/// let value = ValueBag::from_fill(&|slot: Slot| {
[194](https://docs.rs#194)///     #[derive(Debug)]
[195](https://docs.rs#195)///     struct MyShortLivedValue;
[196](https://docs.rs#196)///
[197](https://docs.rs#197)///     slot.fill_debug(&MyShortLivedValue)
[198](https://docs.rs#198)/// });
[199](https://docs.rs#199)///
[200](https://docs.rs#200)/// assert_eq!("MyShortLivedValue", format!("{:?}", value));
[201](https://docs.rs#201)/// ```
[202](https://docs.rs#202)///
[203](https://docs.rs#203)/// The trait can also be implemented manually:
[204](https://docs.rs#204)///
[205](https://docs.rs#205)/// ```
[206](https://docs.rs#206)/// # use std::fmt::Debug;
[207](https://docs.rs#207)/// use value_bag::{ValueBag, Error, fill::{Slot, Fill}};
[208](https://docs.rs#208)///
[209](https://docs.rs#209)/// struct FillDebug;
[210](https://docs.rs#210)///
[211](https://docs.rs#211)/// impl Fill for FillDebug {
[212](https://docs.rs#212)///     fn fill(&self, slot: Slot) -> Result<(), Error> {
[213](https://docs.rs#213)///         slot.fill_debug(&42i32 as &dyn Debug)
[214](https://docs.rs#214)///     }
[215](https://docs.rs#215)/// }
[216](https://docs.rs#216)///
[217](https://docs.rs#217)/// let value = ValueBag::from_fill(&FillDebug);
[218](https://docs.rs#218)///
[219](https://docs.rs#219)/// assert_eq!(None, value.to_i64());
[220](https://docs.rs#220)/// ```
[221](https://docs.rs#221)///
[222](https://docs.rs#222)/// # Inspecting values
[223](https://docs.rs#223)///
[224](https://docs.rs#224)/// Once you have a `ValueBag` there are also a few ways to inspect it:
[225](https://docs.rs#225)///
[226](https://docs.rs#226)/// - Using `std::fmt`
[227](https://docs.rs#227)/// - Using `sval`
[228](https://docs.rs#228)/// - Using `serde`
[229](https://docs.rs#229)/// - Using the `ValueBag::visit` method.
[230](https://docs.rs#230)/// - Using the `ValueBag::to_*` methods.
[231](https://docs.rs#231)/// - Using the `ValueBag::downcast_ref` method.
[232](https://docs.rs#232)///
[233](https://docs.rs#233)/// ## Using the `ValueBag::visit` method
[234](https://docs.rs#234)///
[235](https://docs.rs#235)/// The [`visit`] module provides a simple visitor API that can be used to inspect
[236](https://docs.rs#236)/// the structure of primitives stored in a `ValueBag`.
[237](https://docs.rs#237)/// More complex datatypes can then be handled using `std::fmt`, `sval`, or `serde`.
[238](https://docs.rs#238)///
[239](https://docs.rs#239)/// ```
[240](https://docs.rs#240)/// #[cfg(not(feature = "std"))] fn main() {}
[241](https://docs.rs#241)/// #[cfg(feature = "std")]
[242](https://docs.rs#242)/// # fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
[243](https://docs.rs#243)/// # fn escape(buf: &[u8]) -> &[u8] { buf }
[244](https://docs.rs#244)/// # fn itoa_fmt<T>(num: T) -> Vec<u8> { vec![] }
[245](https://docs.rs#245)/// # fn ryu_fmt<T>(num: T) -> Vec<u8> { vec![] }
[246](https://docs.rs#246)/// # use std::io::Write;
[247](https://docs.rs#247)/// use value_bag::{ValueBag, Error, visit::Visit};
[248](https://docs.rs#248)///
[249](https://docs.rs#249)/// // Implement some simple custom serialization
[250](https://docs.rs#250)/// struct MyVisit(Vec<u8>);
[251](https://docs.rs#251)/// impl<'v> Visit<'v> for MyVisit {
[252](https://docs.rs#252)///     fn visit_any(&mut self, v: ValueBag) -> Result<(), Error> {
[253](https://docs.rs#253)///         // Fallback to `Debug` if we didn't visit the value specially
[254](https://docs.rs#254)///         write!(&mut self.0, "{:?}", v).map_err(|_| Error::msg("failed to write value"))
[255](https://docs.rs#255)///     }
[256](https://docs.rs#256)///
[257](https://docs.rs#257)///     fn visit_u64(&mut self, v: u64) -> Result<(), Error> {
[258](https://docs.rs#258)///         self.0.extend_from_slice(itoa_fmt(v).as_slice());
[259](https://docs.rs#259)///         Ok(())
[260](https://docs.rs#260)///     }
[261](https://docs.rs#261)///
[262](https://docs.rs#262)///     fn visit_i64(&mut self, v: i64) -> Result<(), Error> {
[263](https://docs.rs#263)///         self.0.extend_from_slice(itoa_fmt(v).as_slice());
[264](https://docs.rs#264)///         Ok(())
[265](https://docs.rs#265)///     }
[266](https://docs.rs#266)///
[267](https://docs.rs#267)///     fn visit_f64(&mut self, v: f64) -> Result<(), Error> {
[268](https://docs.rs#268)///         self.0.extend_from_slice(ryu_fmt(v).as_slice());
[269](https://docs.rs#269)///         Ok(())
[270](https://docs.rs#270)///     }
[271](https://docs.rs#271)///
[272](https://docs.rs#272)///     fn visit_str(&mut self, v: &str) -> Result<(), Error> {
[273](https://docs.rs#273)///         self.0.push(b'\"');
[274](https://docs.rs#274)///         self.0.extend_from_slice(escape(v.as_bytes()));
[275](https://docs.rs#275)///         self.0.push(b'\"');
[276](https://docs.rs#276)///         Ok(())
[277](https://docs.rs#277)///     }
[278](https://docs.rs#278)///
[279](https://docs.rs#279)///     fn visit_bool(&mut self, v: bool) -> Result<(), Error> {
[280](https://docs.rs#280)///         self.0.extend_from_slice(if v { b"true" } else { b"false" });
[281](https://docs.rs#281)///         Ok(())
[282](https://docs.rs#282)///     }
[283](https://docs.rs#283)/// }
[284](https://docs.rs#284)///
[285](https://docs.rs#285)/// let value = ValueBag::from(42i64);
[286](https://docs.rs#286)///
[287](https://docs.rs#287)/// let mut visitor = MyVisit(vec![]);
[288](https://docs.rs#288)/// value.visit(&mut visitor)?;
[289](https://docs.rs#289)/// # Ok(())
[290](https://docs.rs#290)/// # }
[291](https://docs.rs#291)/// ```
[292](https://docs.rs#292)///
[293](https://docs.rs#293)/// ## Using `std::fmt`
[294](https://docs.rs#294)///
[295](https://docs.rs#295)/// Any `ValueBag` can be formatted using the `std::fmt` machinery as either `Debug`
[296](https://docs.rs#296)/// or `Display`.
[297](https://docs.rs#297)///
[298](https://docs.rs#298)/// ```
[299](https://docs.rs#299)/// use value_bag::ValueBag;
[300](https://docs.rs#300)///
[301](https://docs.rs#301)/// let value = ValueBag::from(true);
[302](https://docs.rs#302)///
[303](https://docs.rs#303)/// assert_eq!("true", format!("{:?}", value));
[304](https://docs.rs#304)/// ```
[305](https://docs.rs#305)///
[306](https://docs.rs#306)/// ## Using `sval`
[307](https://docs.rs#307)///
[308](https://docs.rs#308)/// When the `sval2` feature is enabled, any `ValueBag` can be serialized using `sval`.
[309](https://docs.rs#309)/// This makes it possible to visit any typed structure captured in the `ValueBag`,
[310](https://docs.rs#310)/// including complex datatypes like maps and sequences.
[311](https://docs.rs#311)///
[312](https://docs.rs#312)/// `sval` doesn't need to allocate so can be used in no-std environments.
[313](https://docs.rs#313)///
[314](https://docs.rs#314)/// First, enable the `sval2` feature in your `Cargo.toml`:
[315](https://docs.rs#315)///
[316](https://docs.rs#316)/// ```toml
[317](https://docs.rs#317)/// [dependencies.value-bag]
[318](https://docs.rs#318)/// features = ["sval2"]
[319](https://docs.rs#319)/// ```
[320](https://docs.rs#320)///
[321](https://docs.rs#321)/// Then stream the contents of the `ValueBag` using `sval`.
[322](https://docs.rs#322)///
[323](https://docs.rs#323)/// ```
[324](https://docs.rs#324)/// # #[cfg(not(all(feature = "std", feature = "sval2")))] fn main() {}
[325](https://docs.rs#325)/// # #[cfg(all(feature = "std", feature = "sval2"))]
[326](https://docs.rs#326)/// # fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
[327](https://docs.rs#327)/// # use value_bag_sval2::json as sval_json;
[328](https://docs.rs#328)/// use value_bag::ValueBag;
[329](https://docs.rs#329)///
[330](https://docs.rs#330)/// let value = ValueBag::from(42i64);
[331](https://docs.rs#331)/// let json = sval_json::stream_to_string(value)?;
[332](https://docs.rs#332)/// # Ok(())
[333](https://docs.rs#333)/// # }
[334](https://docs.rs#334)/// ```
[335](https://docs.rs#335)///
[336](https://docs.rs#336)/// ## Using `serde`
[337](https://docs.rs#337)///
[338](https://docs.rs#338)/// When the `serde1` feature is enabled, any `ValueBag` can be serialized using `serde`.
[339](https://docs.rs#339)/// This makes it possible to visit any typed structure captured in the `ValueBag`,
[340](https://docs.rs#340)/// including complex datatypes like maps and sequences.
[341](https://docs.rs#341)///
[342](https://docs.rs#342)/// `serde` needs a few temporary allocations, so also brings in the `std` feature.
[343](https://docs.rs#343)///
[344](https://docs.rs#344)/// First, enable the `serde1` feature in your `Cargo.toml`:
[345](https://docs.rs#345)///
[346](https://docs.rs#346)/// ```toml
[347](https://docs.rs#347)/// [dependencies.value-bag]
[348](https://docs.rs#348)/// features = ["serde1"]
[349](https://docs.rs#349)/// ```
[350](https://docs.rs#350)///
[351](https://docs.rs#351)/// Then stream the contents of the `ValueBag` using `serde`.
[352](https://docs.rs#352)///
[353](https://docs.rs#353)/// ```
[354](https://docs.rs#354)/// # #[cfg(not(all(feature = "std", feature = "serde1")))] fn main() {}
[355](https://docs.rs#355)/// # #[cfg(all(feature = "std", feature = "serde1"))]
[356](https://docs.rs#356)/// # fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
[357](https://docs.rs#357)/// # use value_bag_serde1::json as serde_json;
[358](https://docs.rs#358)/// use value_bag::ValueBag;
[359](https://docs.rs#359)///
[360](https://docs.rs#360)/// let value = ValueBag::from(42i64);
[361](https://docs.rs#361)/// let json = serde_json::to_string(&value)?;
[362](https://docs.rs#362)/// # Ok(())
[363](https://docs.rs#363)/// # }
[364](https://docs.rs#364)/// ```
[365](https://docs.rs#365)///
[366](https://docs.rs#366)/// Also see [`serde.rs`](https://serde.rs) for more examples of writing your own serializers.
[367](https://docs.rs#367)///
[368](https://docs.rs#368)/// ## Using the `ValueBag::to_*` methods
[369](https://docs.rs#369)///
[370](https://docs.rs#370)/// `ValueBag` provides a set of methods for attempting to pull a concrete value out.
[371](https://docs.rs#371)/// These are useful for ad-hoc analysis but aren't intended for exhaustively serializing
[372](https://docs.rs#372)/// the contents of a `ValueBag`.
[373](https://docs.rs#373)///
[374](https://docs.rs#374)/// ```
[375](https://docs.rs#375)/// use value_bag::ValueBag;
[376](https://docs.rs#376)///
[377](https://docs.rs#377)/// let value = ValueBag::capture_display(&42u64);
[378](https://docs.rs#378)///
[379](https://docs.rs#379)/// assert_eq!(Some(42u64), value.to_u64());
[380](https://docs.rs#380)/// ```
[381](https://docs.rs#381)///
[382](https://docs.rs#382)/// ## Using the `ValueBag::downcast_ref` method
[383](https://docs.rs#383)///
[384](https://docs.rs#384)/// When a `ValueBag` is created using one of the `capture_*` constructors, it can be downcast
[385](https://docs.rs#385)/// back to its original value.
[386](https://docs.rs#386)/// This can also be useful for ad-hoc analysis where there's a common possible non-primitive
[387](https://docs.rs#387)/// type that could be captured.
[388](https://docs.rs#388)///
[389](https://docs.rs#389)/// ```
[390](https://docs.rs#390)/// # #[derive(Debug)] struct SystemTime;
[391](https://docs.rs#391)/// # fn now() -> SystemTime { SystemTime }
[392](https://docs.rs#392)/// use value_bag::ValueBag;
[393](https://docs.rs#393)///
[394](https://docs.rs#394)/// let timestamp = now();
[395](https://docs.rs#395)/// let value = ValueBag::capture_debug(×tamp);
[396](https://docs.rs#396)///
[397](https://docs.rs#397)/// assert!(value.downcast_ref::<SystemTime>().is_some());
[398](https://docs.rs#398)/// ```
[399](https://docs.rs#399)///
[400](https://docs.rs#400)/// # Working with sequences
[401](https://docs.rs#401)///
[402](https://docs.rs#402)/// The `seq` feature of `value-bag` enables utilities for working with values that are sequences.
[403](https://docs.rs#403)/// First, enable the `seq` feature in your `Cargo.toml`:
[404](https://docs.rs#404)///
[405](https://docs.rs#405)/// ```toml
[406](https://docs.rs#406)/// [dependencies.value-bag]
[407](https://docs.rs#407)/// features = ["seq"]
[408](https://docs.rs#408)/// ```
[409](https://docs.rs#409)///
[410](https://docs.rs#410)/// Slices and arrays can be captured as sequences:
[411](https://docs.rs#411)///
[412](https://docs.rs#412)/// ```
[413](https://docs.rs#413)/// # #[cfg(not(all(feature = "serde1", feature = "seq")))] fn main() {}
[414](https://docs.rs#414)/// # #[cfg(all(feature = "serde1", feature = "seq"))]
[415](https://docs.rs#415)/// # fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
[416](https://docs.rs#416)/// # use value_bag_serde1::json as serde_json;
[417](https://docs.rs#417)/// use value_bag::ValueBag;
[418](https://docs.rs#418)///
[419](https://docs.rs#419)/// let value = ValueBag::from_seq_slice(&[1, 2, 3]);
[420](https://docs.rs#420)///
[421](https://docs.rs#421)/// assert_eq!("[1,2,3]", serde_json::to_string(&value)?);
[422](https://docs.rs#422)/// # Ok(())
[423](https://docs.rs#423)/// # }
[424](https://docs.rs#424)/// ```
[425](https://docs.rs#425)///
[426](https://docs.rs#426)/// A sequence captured with either `sval` or `serde` can have its elements extracted:
[427](https://docs.rs#427)///
[428](https://docs.rs#428)/// ```
[429](https://docs.rs#429)/// # #[cfg(not(all(feature = "serde1", feature = "seq")))] fn main() {}
[430](https://docs.rs#430)/// # #[cfg(all(feature = "serde1", feature = "seq"))]
[431](https://docs.rs#431)/// # fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
[432](https://docs.rs#432)/// use value_bag::ValueBag;
[433](https://docs.rs#433)///
[434](https://docs.rs#434)/// let value = ValueBag::from_serde1(&[1.0, 2.0, 3.0]);
[435](https://docs.rs#435)///
[436](https://docs.rs#436)/// let seq = value.to_f64_seq::<Vec<Option<f64>>>().ok_or("not a sequence")?;
[437](https://docs.rs#437)///
[438](https://docs.rs#438)/// assert_eq!(vec![Some(1.0), Some(2.0), Some(3.0)], seq);
[439](https://docs.rs#439)/// # Ok(())
[440](https://docs.rs#440)/// # }
[441](https://docs.rs#441)/// ```

# ValueBag in value_bag - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/value-bag/1.12.0/value_bag/struct.ValueBag.html

`pub struct ValueBag<'v> { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

A dynamic structured value.

[§](https://docs.rs#capturing-values)Capturing values

There are a few ways to capture a value:

- Using the `ValueBag::capture_*`and`ValueBag::from_*`methods.
- Using the standard `From`trait.
- Using the `Fill`API.

[§](https://docs.rs#using-the-valuebagcapture_-methods)Using the `ValueBag::capture_*` methods

`ValueBag` offers a few constructor methods that capture values of different kinds.
These methods require a `T: 'static` to support downcasting.

```
use value_bag::ValueBag;
let value = ValueBag::capture_debug(&42i32);
assert_eq!(Some(42), value.to_i64());
```
Capturing a value using these methods will retain type information so that the contents of the bag can be serialized using an appropriate type.

For cases where the `'static` bound can’t be satisfied, there’s also a few
constructors that exclude it.

```
use value_bag::ValueBag;
let value = ValueBag::from_debug(&42i32);
assert_eq!(None, value.to_i64());
```
These `ValueBag::from_*` methods are lossy though and `ValueBag::capture_*` should be preferred.

[§](https://docs.rs#using-the-standard-from-trait)Using the standard `From` trait

Primitive types can be converted into a `ValueBag` using the standard `From` trait.

```
use value_bag::ValueBag;
let value = ValueBag::from(42i32);
assert_eq!(Some(42), value.to_i64());
```
[§](https://docs.rs#using-the-fill-api)Using the `Fill` API

The [ fill](https://docs.rs/fill/index.html) module provides a way to bridge APIs that may not be directly
compatible with other constructor methods.

The `Fill` trait is automatically implemented for closures, so can usually
be used in libraries that can’t implement the trait themselves.

```
use value_bag::{ValueBag, fill::Slot};
let value = ValueBag::from_fill(&|slot: Slot| {
    #[derive(Debug)]
    struct MyShortLivedValue;
    slot.fill_debug(&MyShortLivedValue)
});
assert_eq!("MyShortLivedValue", format!("{:?}", value));
```
The trait can also be implemented manually:

```
use value_bag::{ValueBag, Error, fill::{Slot, Fill}};
struct FillDebug;
impl Fill for FillDebug {
    fn fill(&self, slot: Slot) -> Result<(), Error> {
        slot.fill_debug(&42i32 as &dyn Debug)
    }
}
let value = ValueBag::from_fill(&FillDebug);
assert_eq!(None, value.to_i64());
```
[§](https://docs.rs#inspecting-values)Inspecting values

Once you have a `ValueBag` there are also a few ways to inspect it:

- Using `std::fmt`
- Using `sval`
- Using `serde`
- Using the `ValueBag::visit`method.
- Using the `ValueBag::to_*`methods.
- Using the `ValueBag::downcast_ref`method.

[§](https://docs.rs#using-the-valuebagvisit-method)Using the `ValueBag::visit` method

The [ visit](https://docs.rs/visit/index.html) module provides a simple visitor API that can be used to inspect
the structure of primitives stored in a

`ValueBag`.
More complex datatypes can then be handled using `std::fmt`, `sval`, or `serde`.```
#[cfg(not(feature = "std"))] fn main() {}
#[cfg(feature = "std")]
use value_bag::{ValueBag, Error, visit::Visit};
// Implement some simple custom serialization
struct MyVisit(Vec<u8>);
impl<'v> Visit<'v> for MyVisit {
    fn visit_any(&mut self, v: ValueBag) -> Result<(), Error> {
        // Fallback to `Debug` if we didn't visit the value specially
        write!(&mut self.0, "{:?}", v).map_err(|_| Error::msg("failed to write value"))
    }
    fn visit_u64(&mut self, v: u64) -> Result<(), Error> {
        self.0.extend_from_slice(itoa_fmt(v).as_slice());
        Ok(())
    }
    fn visit_i64(&mut self, v: i64) -> Result<(), Error> {
        self.0.extend_from_slice(itoa_fmt(v).as_slice());
        Ok(())
    }
    fn visit_f64(&mut self, v: f64) -> Result<(), Error> {
        self.0.extend_from_slice(ryu_fmt(v).as_slice());
        Ok(())
    }
    fn visit_str(&mut self, v: &str) -> Result<(), Error> {
        self.0.push(b'\"');
        self.0.extend_from_slice(escape(v.as_bytes()));
        self.0.push(b'\"');
        Ok(())
    }
    fn visit_bool(&mut self, v: bool) -> Result<(), Error> {
        self.0.extend_from_slice(if v { b"true" } else { b"false" });
        Ok(())
    }
}
let value = ValueBag::from(42i64);
let mut visitor = MyVisit(vec![]);
value.visit(&mut visitor)?;
```
[§](https://docs.rs#using-stdfmt)Using `std::fmt`

Any `ValueBag` can be formatted using the `std::fmt` machinery as either `Debug`
or `Display`.

```
use value_bag::ValueBag;
let value = ValueBag::from(true);
assert_eq!("true", format!("{:?}", value));
```
[§](https://docs.rs#using-sval)Using `sval`

When the `sval2` feature is enabled, any `ValueBag` can be serialized using `sval`.
This makes it possible to visit any typed structure captured in the `ValueBag`,
including complex datatypes like maps and sequences.

`sval` doesn’t need to allocate so can be used in no-std environments.

First, enable the `sval2` feature in your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[dependencies.value-bag]
features = ["sval2"]
```
Then stream the contents of the `ValueBag` using `sval`.

```
use value_bag::ValueBag;
let value = ValueBag::from(42i64);
let json = sval_json::stream_to_string(value)?;
```
[§](https://docs.rs#using-serde)Using `serde`

When the `serde1` feature is enabled, any `ValueBag` can be serialized using `serde`.
This makes it possible to visit any typed structure captured in the `ValueBag`,
including complex datatypes like maps and sequences.

`serde` needs a few temporary allocations, so also brings in the `std` feature.

First, enable the `serde1` feature in your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[dependencies.value-bag]
features = ["serde1"]
```
Then stream the contents of the `ValueBag` using `serde`.

```
use value_bag::ValueBag;
let value = ValueBag::from(42i64);
let json = serde_json::to_string(&value)?;
```
Also see [ serde.rs](https://serde.rs) for more examples of writing your own serializers.

[§](https://docs.rs#using-the-valuebagto_-methods)Using the `ValueBag::to_*` methods

`ValueBag` provides a set of methods for attempting to pull a concrete value out.
These are useful for ad-hoc analysis but aren’t intended for exhaustively serializing
the contents of a `ValueBag`.

```
use value_bag::ValueBag;
let value = ValueBag::capture_display(&42u64);
assert_eq!(Some(42u64), value.to_u64());
```
[§](https://docs.rs#using-the-valuebagdowncast_ref-method)Using the `ValueBag::downcast_ref` method

When a `ValueBag` is created using one of the `capture_*` constructors, it can be downcast
back to its original value.
This can also be useful for ad-hoc analysis where there’s a common possible non-primitive
type that could be captured.

```
use value_bag::ValueBag;
let timestamp = now();
let value = ValueBag::capture_debug(×tamp);
assert!(value.downcast_ref::<SystemTime>().is_some());
```
[§](https://docs.rs#working-with-sequences)Working with sequences

The `seq` feature of `value-bag` enables utilities for working with values that are sequences.
First, enable the `seq` feature in your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[dependencies.value-bag]
features = ["seq"]
```
Slices and arrays can be captured as sequences:

```
use value_bag::ValueBag;
let value = ValueBag::from_seq_slice(&[1, 2, 3]);
assert_eq!("[1,2,3]", serde_json::to_string(&value)?);
```
A sequence captured with either `sval` or `serde` can have its elements extracted:

```
use value_bag::ValueBag;
let value = ValueBag::from_serde1(&[1.0, 2.0, 3.0]);
let seq = value.to_f64_seq::<Vec<Option<f64>>>().ok_or("not a sequence")?;
assert_eq!(vec![Some(1.0), Some(2.0), Some(3.0)], seq);
```

# value_bag::fill - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/value-bag/1.12.0/value_bag/fill/index.html

## Expand description

Deferred value initialization.

The [ Fill](https://docs.rs/trait.Fill.html) trait is a way to bridge APIs that may not be directly
compatible with other constructor methods.

The `Fill` trait is automatically implemented for closures, so can usually
be used in libraries that can’t implement the trait themselves.

```
use value_bag::{ValueBag, fill::Slot};
let value = ValueBag::from_fill(&|slot: Slot| {
    #[derive(Debug)]
    struct MyShortLivedValue;
    slot.fill_debug(&MyShortLivedValue)
});
assert_eq!("MyShortLivedValue", format!("{:?}", value));
```
The trait can also be implemented manually:

```
use value_bag::{ValueBag, Error, fill::{Slot, Fill}};
struct FillDebug;
impl Fill for FillDebug {
    fn fill(&self, slot: Slot) -> Result<(), Error> {
        slot.fill_debug(&42i64 as &dyn Debug)
    }
}
let value = ValueBag::from_fill(&FillDebug);
assert_eq!(None, value.to_i64());
```

# value_bag::visit - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/value-bag/1.12.0/value_bag/visit/index.html

## Expand description

Value inspection.

The [ Visit](https://docs.rs/trait.Visit.html) trait provides a simple visitor API that can be used to inspect
the structure of primitives stored in a

[. More complex datatypes can then be handled using](https://docs.rs/struct.ValueBag.html)

`ValueBag``std::fmt`, `sval`, or `serde`.```
use value_bag::{ValueBag, Error, visit::Visit};
// Implement some simple custom serialization
struct MyVisit(Vec<u8>);
impl<'v> Visit<'v> for MyVisit {
    fn visit_any(&mut self, v: ValueBag) -> Result<(), Error> {
        // Fallback to `Debug` if we didn't visit the value specially
        write!(&mut self.0, "{:?}", v).map_err(|_| Error::msg("failed to write value"))
    }
    fn visit_u64(&mut self, v: u64) -> Result<(), Error> {
        self.0.extend_from_slice(itoa_fmt(v).as_slice());
        Ok(())
    }
    fn visit_i64(&mut self, v: i64) -> Result<(), Error> {
        self.0.extend_from_slice(itoa_fmt(v).as_slice());
        Ok(())
    }
    fn visit_f64(&mut self, v: f64) -> Result<(), Error> {
        self.0.extend_from_slice(ryu_fmt(v).as_slice());
        Ok(())
    }
    fn visit_str(&mut self, v: &str) -> Result<(), Error> {
        self.0.push(b'\"');
        self.0.extend_from_slice(escape(v.as_bytes()));
        self.0.push(b'\"');
        Ok(())
    }
    fn visit_bool(&mut self, v: bool) -> Result<(), Error> {
        self.0.extend_from_slice(if v { b"true" } else { b"false" });
        Ok(())
    }
}
let value = ValueBag::from(42i64);
let mut visitor = MyVisit(vec![]);
value.visit(&mut visitor)?;
```
## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Visit](https://docs.rs/trait.Visit.html)
- A visitor for a `ValueBag`.

# OwnedValueBag in value_bag - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/value-bag/1.12.0/value_bag/struct.OwnedValueBag.html

Struct OwnedValueBag    Copy item path  Source  `pub struct OwnedValueBag {  }`Expand description A dynamic structured value.

This type is an owned variant of `ValueBag``to_owned``OwnedValueBag`s are suitable for storing and sharing across threads.

`OwnedValueBag`s can be inspected by converting back into a regular `ValueBag`
using the `by_ref`

Get a regular `ValueBag`

Once a `ValueBag` has been buffered, it will behave
slightly differently when converted back:

`fmt::Debug` won’t use formatting flags.`serde::Serialize` will use the text-based representation.The original type may change, so downcasting can stop producing results.

Make this value cheap to clone and share by internally storing it in an `Arc`.

If the value is already shared then this method will simply clone it.

Performs copy-assignment from

`source`.

# value_bag - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/value-bag/latest/value_bag/

## Expand description

Structured values.

This crate contains the [ ValueBag](https://docs.rs/struct.ValueBag.html) type, a container for an anonymous structured value.

`ValueBag`s can be captured in various ways and then formatted, inspected, and serialized
without losing their original structure.The producer of a [ ValueBag](https://docs.rs/struct.ValueBag.html) may use a different strategy for capturing than the eventual
consumer. They don’t need to coordinate directly.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Error](https://docs.rs/struct.Error.html)
- An error encountered while working with structured data.
- [Owned](https://docs.rs/struct.OwnedValueBag.html)- Value - Bag
- A dynamic structured value.
- [Value](https://docs.rs/struct.ValueBag.html)- Bag
- A dynamic structured value.

# wasm-bindgen 0.2.126 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/wasm-bindgen/^0.2

Built with 🦀🕸 by The Rust and WebAssembly Working Group

## Install `wasm-bindgen-cli`

You can install it using `cargo install`:

```
cargo install wasm-bindgen-cli
```
Or, you can download it from the
[release page](https://github.com/wasm-bindgen/wasm-bindgen/releases).

If you have [ cargo-binstall](https://crates.io/crates/cargo-binstall) installed,
then you can install the pre-built artifacts by running:

```
cargo binstall wasm-bindgen-cli
```
## Example

Import JavaScript things into Rust and export Rust things to JavaScript.

```
use *;
// Import the `window.alert` function from the Web.
extern "C"
// Export a `greet` function from Rust to JavaScript, that alerts a
// hello message.
```
Use exported Rust things from JavaScript with ECMAScript modules!

```
import  from "./hello_world";
;
```
## Features

-
**Lightweight.**Only pay for what you use.`wasm-bindgen`only generates bindings and glue for the JavaScript imports you actually use and Rust functionality that you export. For example, importing and using the`document.querySelector`method doesn't cause`Node.prototype.appendChild`or`window.alert`to be included in the bindings as well.
-
**ECMAScript modules.**Just import WebAssembly modules the same way you would import JavaScript modules. Future compatible with[WebAssembly modules and ECMAScript modules integration](https://github.com/WebAssembly/esm-integration).
-
**Designed with the**Eventually, there won't be any JavaScript shims between Rust-generated wasm functions and native DOM methods. Because the Wasm functions are statically type checked, some of those native methods' dynamic type checks should become unnecessary, promising to unlock even-faster-than-JavaScript DOM access.["Web IDL bindings" proposal](https://github.com/WebAssembly/proposals/issues/8)in mind.

## Guide

## API Docs

## MSRV Policy

- Libraries that are released on [crates.io](https://crates.io)have a MSRV of v1.77.
- CLI tools and their corresponding support libraries have a MSRV of v1.86.

The project aims to maintain a 2-year MSRV policy for libraries (meaning we support Rust versions released within the last 2 years), but with a shorter MSRV policy for the CLI. Changes to the MSRV may be made in patch versions, and will be logged in the CHANGELOG and MSRV history below.

### MSRV History

| Version | Library MSRV | CLI MSRV | Date |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0.2.118 | 1.77 | 1.86 | 2026-04-10 |
| 0.2.106 | 1.71 | 1.82 | 2025-11-27 |
| 0.2.103 | 1.57 | 1.82 | 2025-09-17 |
| 0.2.93 | 1.57 | 1.76 | 2024-08-13 |
